question: to the Commission Nikos Pappas (The Left) Subject:

Recent incidents in Greece have highlighted signs that teachers are being inadequately protected against violence and psychosocial pressures. In particular, investigations are being carried out into the death of a teacher in Thessaloniki, with reports of intimidation in the school environment, and the death of a head teacher at a school in Athens, with witnesses claiming she had been put under intense mental stress. There is also publicly available audiovisual material pointing to threatening attitudes towards teachers. Similar incidents in other Member States suggest a broader European dimension, raising questions about the adequacy of existing prevention and protection mechanisms, both at national and European level. The Charter of Fundamental Rights of the European Union enshrines the right to dignity and safe working conditions. Directive 89/391/EEC requires that occupational risks, including psychosocial risks, be prevented and the European Pillar of Social Rights provides for a high level of protection of workers’ health and safety. In view of the above, can the Commission answer the following: 1.
Does it have comparative data on the extent of the violence and psychosocial risks that exist in the field of education?
What is its assessment of the existing health and safety framework in school environments?
Does it intend to take initiatives to boost prevention and teacher protection?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (20.7.2026) The 2024 European Survey of Enterprises on New and Emerging Risks1 of the European Agency on Safety and Health at Work provides data on psychosocial risks at work by sector and country. In Greece, 85% of respondents in the education sector reported having to deal with difficult customers, patients, pupils – one of the highest rates in the EU. Eurostat collects annual data on reported non-fatal and fatal accidents at work across all economic sectors. In the education sector in Greece, no fatal2 accidents were reported for 2014-2023. The number of non-fatal cases3 rose from 42 in 2021 to 54 in 2023. The Commission is working with stakeholders to find solutions for this complex topic. The Framework Directive on Safety and Health at Work4 covers all occupational risks and lays down the main principles of prevention and protection against them. This Directive applies to all sectors of activity, including education, and it is up to Member States to properly and effectively transpose it. As part of the envisaged Quality Jobs Act, the Commission is carrying out a review of the Workplace Directive5 and Display Screen Directive6. EU action, applicable also to education, would strive to reconcile the need to improve worker protection in light of the digital transition, while avoiding unnecessary burden on companies and simplifying the legislation. Issues to be addressed would include better addressing the psychosocial risks, among others. In the field of education, the Commission supports teacher safety by promoting safe, inclusive school environments and whole-school measures to prevent school violence, bullying and harassment7. The envisaged EU Teachers and Trainers Agenda announced in the Union of Skills would also cover teachers’ working conditions.
